title: Wall Balls: The Movement Everyone Underestimates
excerpt: Wall balls look easy until rep 40. How to set up the squat, time the throw, choose a target height and ball weight, and pace your sets.
description: Wall balls look easy until rep 40. How to set up the squat, time the throw, pick a target height and ball weight, and breathe so you can keep going in a WOD.

toc.title: Throw With Your Legs, Not Your Arms

bodyHtml:
Why Wall Balls Fool People

On paper, a wall ball is a squat and a throw with a light ball. Twenty pounds for men, fourteen for women, thrown to a ten-foot or nine-foot target. Nothing about it looks scary, so people treat it as the easy part of a workout. Then the set of 50 arrives, the ball starts feeling like a bowling ball, and the walk back to the wall gets longer.

The reason is that the movement chains two big efforts together with almost no pause: a full squat and a hard push overhead. Your legs, hips, shoulders, and breathing all get taxed at once. Done well, the legs do most of the lifting and the arms just steer. Done badly, the shoulders do all of it and you are finished by rep 30.

"Wall balls are cheap to start and expensive to finish. The athletes who look relaxed at rep 60 set up well at rep 1."

Start With a Real Squat

Stand about a foot back from the wall, feet shoulder-width or a little wider, toes turned out slightly. Hold the ball at your chest with your elbows under it, not flared. Sit down until your hip crease passes below your knee. Most no-reps happen here, and most fatigue-driven shortcuts do too: the squat gets a little shallower every round.

Keep your chest up and let the ball ride high so your torso stays upright. If your heels lift or your chest falls forward, widen the stance a bit or move closer to the wall. A quick check on your air squat depth before the workout tells you a lot about what you will do under fatigue. The wall ball movement page has the full standard and demo.

Throw With Your Legs, Not Your Arms

The throw starts as you stand. Drive out of the bottom of the squat and let that momentum travel up through your hips into the ball. By the time your legs are nearly straight, your hands should be pushing the ball up the wall in one smooth line. Your arms finish the throw; they do not start it.

Look at the target, not the ball. Pick a spot on the wall and aim for the same spot every rep. Catch the ball as it comes down with your arms soft, let it carry you straight into the next squat, and keep your elbows tucked. Catching at the bottom of the squat instead of standing and resetting is what makes wall balls cycle quickly. It is also what makes them feel brutal, so practice it in smaller sets before a long one.

Target Height and Ball Weight

The Rx standard is a 20-pound ball to a 10-foot target for men and a 14-pound ball to a 9-foot target for women. Those are good numbers to aim for, not a requirement. In a garage you may not have a ten-foot wall that is clear and solid, or a ball that matches, so adjust the setup honestly.

If you scale, scale one thing at a time. Drop the ball weight, or lower the target a few inches, but keep full-depth squats. A 14-pound ball to a 9-foot line that you can keep moving beats a 20-pound ball that you drop and chase. Mark your target with tape so the height is the same on retest day. If you need a ball, a medicine ball with a slightly soft shell is gentler on walls and hands than a hard one.

No wall? No problem. Throw to a line of tape on a garage door, or use a basement wall and a chalk mark. If you have no suitable wall at all, ball slams or thrusters with a light dumbbell hit a similar pattern.

Breathing and Breaking Up Sets

Breathe with the movement: in as you go down, out as you throw. It sounds minor, but holding your breath is one of the fastest ways to gas out. When a set gets long, plan the breaks before you need them. Fifty reps might be 20, 15, 10, 5, or 15 and 10 and 10 and 15, depending on how the workout is built.

The rule is to rest while you are still moving well, not after your form has fallen apart. A short pause of two or three breaths with the ball held at your chest beats dropping it and walking away. Plan your sets the same way you would for a long bodyweight piece like Cindy: steady early, and no hero rounds at the start.

Final Thoughts

Wall balls reward patience. Squat to full depth, drive from the legs, aim at one spot, and break the set before you have to. Do that and the movement goes from the part of the workout you dread to a place where you can make up time.

To practice them in context, the WOD Builder can put wall balls into a workout that fits your gear, and the Daily 20 is there when you only have a short window.
